item.title: Democratic United Front demands judicial probe into Rangpur killings
item.description:
A left-leaning political alliance staged a protest in Rangpur on Monday demanding a judicial inquiry into the killing of four members of a family, including a former teacher of Rangpur Zilla School, and the arrest of those responsible.
The Democratic United Front organised a procession, human chain and rally in the city, alleging that contradictory statements from police had raised questions about the investigation and eroded public confidence in the authorities.
The procession started near the Rangpur Press Club and passed through several major roads before protesters formed a human chain and held a rally in Kachari Bazar, outside the office of the Deputy Commissioner.
Abdul Quddus, Rangpur district coordinator of the Democratic United Front and district convener of the Socialist Party of Bangladesh (SPB), presided over the rally. Kafi Sarker, general secretary of the Rangpur district committee of the Communist Party of Bangladesh (CPB), moderated the event.
Speakers included Abdullah Kafi Ratan, general secretary of the CPB and central coordinator of the Democratic United Front, Nazmul Haque Pradhan, general secretary of Bangladesh Jasad, Bazlur Rashid Firoz, general secretary of SPB and coordinator of the Anti-Imperialist Alliance Sima Dutta of SPB (Marxist), Iqbal Kabir Jahid, general secretary of the Revolutionary Communist League of Bangladesh and Marxist leader Anwar Hossain Bablu.
Ganapati Chakraborty, a former teacher of Rangpur Zilla School, and three members of his family were found killed at their home in Machuapara in Rangpur city.
Police have arrested two suspects, identified by the protesters as Mugdha and Siddhartha Das, in connection with the case. The protesters said police had claimed that the two suspects killed the victims by strangulation after being prevented from using yaba.
The protesters questioned that account, saying drug tests reportedly found no evidence of drug use among the arrested suspects. They also alleged that investigators had not adequately examined possible motives behind the killings.
“The police investigation has lost its credibility among the people,” the speakers said, calling for the case to be investigated under the supervision of a judicial inquiry committee.
They also demanded that the actual perpetrators be identified and arrested and that all possible motives behind the killings be investigated.
The speakers expressed concern over the growing availability of illegal drugs in Rangpur, alleging that drug hotspots and those involved in drug distribution could not be unknown to law-enforcement agencies. They urged the authorities to identify drug suppliers and their alleged patrons and take effective legal action.
They said rising incidents of murder, rape, extortion, robbery and drug-related crime were making people's lives increasingly insecure in Rangpur and elsewhere in Bangladesh.
The protesters warned that failure to ensure a credible investigation and bring the actual killers to justice would lead to stronger protests in Rangpur and across the country.

item.title: Modern cold storage facility nears completion in Bandarban
item.description:
A modern cold storage facility is nearing completion in Bandarban town, offering a much-needed solution to the annual loss of seasonal fruits and vegetables caused by inadequate storage facilities.
The facility, the first of its kind in the district headquarters, is being constructed by the Bandarban unit of the Chattogram Hill Tracts Development Board (CHTDB) at a cost of Tk 1.85 crore and 56 lakh.
Located in the bus station area of Bandarban town, the cold storage will have a capacity to preserve 50 metric tonnes of fruits and other agricultural produce. Construction of the building has largely been completed, while a generator, electrical connections, cooling equipment and other necessary facilities have been installed.
Officials involved in the project said around 95 percent of the work has already been completed and the facility is expected to become operational soon.
Every year, farmers in Bandarban suffer significant financial losses as large quantities of seasonal fruits and vegetables deteriorate because of the lack of proper storage facilities. The new cold storage is expected to reduce post-harvest losses and allow farmers to store their produce until market conditions become more favourable.
Farmers hope the facility will enable them to avoid distress sales during peak harvesting seasons and secure fair prices for their produce.
Abdus Sattar, a farmer from Bandarban Sadar, said the facility would be a major benefit for local growers.
“Although it has taken a long time, we are happy that a cold storage facility is finally being built. Once it becomes operational, we will be able to preserve our agricultural produce and get better prices,” he said.
Lal Piyan Bom, a mango grower from Bandarban Sadar, said the district produces large quantities of Rangwai mangoes and other fruits.
“Bandarban has considerable potential for fruit cultivation. If we have proper storage facilities, we can preserve the fruits and sell them later at better prices,” he said.
According to project sources, construction began in 2023 and is scheduled for completion in 2026.
Abu Bin Mohammad Yasir Arafat, executive engineer of the Bandarban unit of the Chattogram Hill Tracts Development Board, said the project was progressing as planned.
“About 95 percent of the work has already been completed. Once the cold storage becomes operational, farmers will be able to preserve their fruits and other produce for longer periods and earn more from their sales,” he said.

item.title: Power outage disrupts services at Barisal hospital
item.description:
Frequent power outages are causing patients to suffer at Barisal General Hospital and Sher-e-Bangla Medical College Hospital (SBMCH), disrupting treatment and making it difficult to keep operating theatres and critical care units running.
Patients at the hospital face three to four hours of load shedding a day, according to hospital authorities and patients’ relatives.
The department operates from a five-storey building where about 400 patients are admitted on average each day, accompanied by more than 500 relatives, hospital officials said.
When electricity fails, ceiling fans stop working and the crowded wards quickly become difficult to tolerate, particularly for patients suffering from breathing difficulties and other serious illnesses.
“Because of the large number of patients and relatives, it is already very hot inside,” said Abdul Qayum, who has been staying at the hospital with his daughter for seven days. “When the power goes out repeatedly, it feels like we are being boiled.”
Qayum said he bought a rechargeable fan and brought two hand fans to keep his daughter comfortable.
Hospital Director Brigadier General A.K.M. Mashiul Munir said the Medicine Department is served by a single electricity line, unlike the main hospital building, which has two lines and experiences little load-shedding.
“We have requested the Public Works Department to supply 100 litres of fuel every day,” Munir said. But the department has told hospital authorities that there is no government allocation for generator fuel.
The hospital has repeatedly appealed to the ministry for funding, he said.
“The generator is ready, and if we receive fuel, we will be able to provide backup power and reduce the patients’ suffering,” Munir said.
He could not say when the fuel would be available.
Md Faisal Alam, executive engineer at the Barisal Public Works Department, confirmed that the ministry does not currently allocate funds for fuel to operate the hospital generator.
“We have applied for an allocation. Once the allocation is received, fuel will be supplied through a contractor,” Alam said.
He also could not provide a timeframe for the funding.
Power outages are a particular concern in the hospital’s intensive care unit, where staff must closely monitor critically ill patients whenever electricity fails.
“We become worried about the patients when the power goes out,” a nurse working in the ICU said. “As soon as load-shedding begins, we have to remain extra vigilant.”
Relatives often help by arranging rechargeable fans and other necessities during outages, nurses said.
Patients and their families also face practical difficulties beyond the heat. Rahima Begum, who is staying with her husband on the fifth floor, said power cuts disable the hospital’s lift, forcing her to use the stairs whenever she needs to collect food or medicine.
“We came here to make my husband better, but now we are becoming sick ourselves,” she said.
The Barisal electricity grid is supplying only 50 to 55 megawatts against demand of around 85 to 90 megawatts, according to officials at the grid control room.
Officials said the hospital’s main building is protected from regular load-shedding because it has two electricity connections. The Medicine Department building, with only one connection, is subjected to several hours of outages.
The shortage has exposed vulnerabilities in a hospital that serves hundreds of patients each day. Without fuel for its backup generator, a critical department is left without electricity for hours at a time.
For patients struggling with illness in extreme heat, the simplest of cooling devices have become essential: rechargeable fans and hand fans.

item.title: DMCH doctor assault: Two accused placed on 3-day remand
item.description:
A Dhaka court on Monday placed two youths on three-day remand each in a case filed over allegedly assaulting, threatening and demanding extortion from Dhaka Medical College Hospital Professor Dr Md Asadur Rahman.
The accused are Sabbir Hossain, 18, and Fahim Israk Labib, 20.
Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Ariful Islam passed the order after a hearing in the afternoon. Rokonuzzaman, inspector of the prosecution department, confirmed the matter.
Earlier, Paltan Model Police Station Sub-Inspector Md Atikuzzaman, also the case’s investigating officer, produced the accused before the court and sought 10 days’ remand for each.
According to the remand plea, the accused are active members of an extortion gang operating at various locations in Dhaka and were directly or indirectly involved in the incident. Police said their custodial interrogation was necessary for a proper and impartial investigation.
According to the case statement, Dr Asadur was leaving his chamber at Popular Diagnostic Centre in the capital’s Shantinagar area around 10:00pm on August 17 when he boarded a CNG-run auto-rickshaw.
Shortly after the vehicle started moving, four people intercepted it and demanded that the door be opened. Although the driver was initially told not to open it, he eventually did so.
The assailants then repeatedly beat the doctor, leaving him injured on the head, above both eyes and on various parts of his body.
Hearing his cries, people nearby rushed to the scene and detained one of the suspects, identified as Jibon, while the others fled.
Police from Paltan Model Police Station rescued the doctor and took him to Dhaka Medical College Hospital.
Dr Asadur filed the case with Paltan Police Station on August 18.

item.title: Promotions in public universities and the question of accountability
item.description:
A crucial question pervades the public university spheres: when a public university makes a decision that affects a faculty member’s career, livelihood, or professional standing, who is actually accountable for that decision? The most likely answer, is nobody in particular.

This is a structural reality at Bangladeshi public universities. Bangladesh has around sixty public universities, all of them created by Acts of Parliament, funded by the state, and governed by statutes that define how they must function, hence can be called statutory institutions. This legal architecture should make them among the most accountable institutions in the country, however, in practice, often the gap between what the law requires and what actually happens inside these institutions, is wide.

Let’s take the matter of academic promotion. Every public university has a set of prescribed criteria for promotion. This is often amended and updated, responding to the academic landscape and ratified by the respective governing bodies such as the syndicate and the academic council.

These criteria exist precisely to ensure that the process is objective, consistent, and insulated from personal discretion. A faculty member who meets those criteria has a legitimate professional interest in being assessed fairly against them. Under Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution of Bangladesh, every citizen is entitled to equal protection of the law and equality of opportunity in public employment. Promotion in a public university is public employment. These constitutional guarantees are enforceable and not simply decorative.

Here some crucial queries arise: what happens when a promotion process goes wrong? When a review board applies criteria that are not in the university’s own ordinance? When documentary evidence that was officially solicited is then disregarded at the point of decision with no explanation? When the outcome is neither communicated nor explained to the applicant for months, despite repeated formal and written requests? What legal remedy exists, and how accessible is it to the aggrieved individuals?

The answer, again, is that the remedy exists in law but is distant in practice. Article 102 of the Constitution gives every citizen the right to approach the High Court Division of the Supreme Court when a public authority acts unlawfully or in violation of fundamental rights. The principles of natural justice, which are part of Bangladesh’s common law, require that any body making a decision affecting an individual’s rights must hear that person’s case, consider the evidence before it, and not act on grounds that are extraneous, prejudicial or invented. These are legally binding requirements, and courts have enforcing authority against public universities in Bangladesh.

A faculty member who wants to challenge a promotion decision fearing unfair assessment of their credentials must retain an advocate, file a writ petition before the High Court, survive the procedural complexity of rule nisi proceedings, and wait for a case to be heard on a busy court docket. This can take months. In the meantime, salary differentials accumulate, career development opportunities pass, and the professional consequences of the original wrong compound quietly with every passing month, not to mention the usual collegial harassments, peer frowning, and mental trauma. The path is arduous.

An example of academic fairness in promotion and appeal procedure can be drawn from one of the world’s top universities (UNSW Sydney), reputed for its academic excellence and procedural transparency. At the University of New South Wales in Australia, for instance, academic staff have a formal right to appeal any adverse promotion decision on procedural fairness grounds within ten working days of notification.

The July Uprising of 2024 created a strong public demand for accountability, transparency, and an end to discrimination and arbitrary authority in Bangladesh. Universities led by new leadership have a responsibility to transform this momentum into meaningful institutional reform

A designated senior officer investigates the appeal, issues a written outcome, and, if procedural irregularity is found to have materially affected the result, returns the application for fresh consideration. Unsuccessful candidates are also entitled to formal written feedback as a matter of course. It is what procedural fairness looks like when it is taken seriously as an institutional obligation rather than a discretionary convention.

The lack of any substantial, effective, and publicly available grievance policy is another serious governance loophole among Bangladeshi public universities, leading to numerous structural and prejudicial injustices. Some private universities are developing such grievance policies, including universities like East West University, an example that public universities must follow to ensure academic fairness and avoid instances of micro injustices happening at the university level that often skip national attention.    

The UGC, as the statutory regulator, exists, among other purposes, to ensure that public universities comply with their own governing statutes and maintain standards of academic governance. It has the authority to investigate complaints against universities and to recommend corrective action or internal resolutions. But there is currently no clear, published, accessible mechanism through which an individual faculty member can bring a specific complaint of procedural unfairness to the UGC and expect a defined process of investigation and response.

Gladly enough, something is better than nothing: there is a sketchy portal on the UGC website for complaint submission that allows affected individuals to bring matters within UGC’s purview, though it offers little detail on how it handles cases involving procedural irregularities in public university faculty promotions Thus, the oversight framework’s operational machinery, in this area at least, remains underdeveloped.

The framework of genuine accountability starts with something very simple: written reasons. When a promotion review board makes an adverse recommendation, the affected applicant should receive a formal written statement explaining which criteria were applied, how each qualifying item was assessed, and on what specific ground any submitted documentation was found insufficient. This is a standard practice in universities with well-developed higher education systems. It is also what the principles of natural justice require. An applicant who does not know why they were turned down cannot effectively challenge the decision, cannot learn from the process, and cannot have any confidence that the process was fair.

In many Bangladeshi public universities, the specific standards applied in promotion decisions are not publicly notified in a manner accessible to faculty members in advance. The ordinance may state the minimum requirements, but the interpretive framework applied by review boards, the weight given to different types of publications, the treatment of interdisciplinary or internationally published work, the standards of evidence expected for forthcoming publications: these are often applied inconsistently and arbitrarily, without prior notice, and without any published precedent that a faculty member could consult.

The July Uprising of 2024 created a strong public demand for accountability, transparency, and an end to discrimination and arbitrary authority in Bangladesh. Universities led by new leadership have a responsibility to transform this momentum into meaningful institutional reform. The accountability structure of promotion reform needs to add three components.

First, a binding obligation to furnish written reasons for all adverse promotion decisions within a defined time period. Second, a publicly notified, transparent framework of promotion criteria, updated regularly to reflect contemporary standards of scholarship, including interdisciplinary research. Third, an accessible, independent internal appeal mechanism that allows a faculty member to challenge an adverse decision before reaching the courts.

All of these measures are consistent with the constitutional framework that governs these institutions. Here, the law is not the problem. The question is whether the institutions that exist within it are willing to be held to it; the willingness is what accountability actually requires.

However, it is not only the fish itself that enjoys popularity; hilsa roe also commands considerable demand and has a thriving market. At the Fishery ghat old fish market in Chattogram, workers undertake an extensive process of carefully removing roe intact from the fish, sorting it and packing it. Depending on size and quality, hilsa roe sells for Tk 3,000 to Tk 4,000 per kilogramme. Packed in ice-filled boxes, the roe is sent to Dhaka and various other parts of the country. This photo story captures the busy scene of hilsa roe collection at fishery ghat.

item.title: Property transfer act will not prevent anyone from following their religion
item.description:
The 1882 ‘Transfer of Property (Amendment) Bill’, concerning the transfer of property, was passed in parliament last Sunday with a provision allowing donors to continue enjoying property they have donated for as long as they remain alive. Various religious organisations, individuals and the Opposition have opposed the law. Law Minister Md Asaduzzaman spoke to Prothom Alo about the issue at the parliament office on Monday. Selim Zahid and Riadul Karim took the interview.

Why was there a need to change the law?

Md Asaduzzaman: The main purpose of enacting the law is that we are witnessing parents becoming helpless in their old age in this society. Even after children have had property transferred to their names, parents are being forced out of their homes. It is from the idea of protecting parents in such situations that this law has been enacted for them.

We are witnessing many parents in society being forced out of their homes after giving their property to their children. Some are suffering from cancer and have property, but the parents are unable even to enjoy their own property. Several years ago, a case came to my attention in which, after a retired major general died, his children had the property transferred to their names. One week later, they threw their mother out of the house.

There are many such small incidents. There are also cases where, after someone dies, other heirs come forward and engage in lawsuits. As a result, while elderly people need protection on the one hand, on the other hand, we are also trying to work on the various avenues for litigation and how such lawsuits can be prevented. It is with this in mind that we brought the law to parliament.

The Opposition said something on Sunday—the Parents’ Maintenance Act of 2013 already exists. So why was this needed again?

Asaduzzaman: This has been introduced anew. The reason is that under the Maintenance Act, parents have to file a case in court. Given our social culture, parents do not easily want to lodge lawsuits against their children. So we do not want to put parents in such a vulnerable position in the later stages of their lives. From the Islamic perspective as well, respecting and taking care of parents is one of the fundamental responsibilities of children.

Here, there are two things in the law. One is the corpus, which we refer to as the principal or ownership. Ownership, however, is being transferred to the child, who is the recipient. The other is usufruct. The literal meaning of usufruct is to enjoy or use someone else’s property. In other words, once the gift is completed, the child becomes the owner. The parents will enjoy the property as the usufructuary. This is permitted in Islam.

As the law minister, what do you consider the most important change in this bill, and what direct impact will it have on people’s lives?

Asaduzzaman: I am receiving calls and messages from many people. They are saying that this is a landmark law. The way this law has been enacted to protect helpless elderly parents in Bangladesh means it will be remembered as a landmark law. It is also a progressive law. Even Shishir Monir, a Jamaat-aligned lawyer, sent me a message about this.

What did he send?

Asaduzzaman: He said that he personally did not find anything wrong with this law.

But the Opposition raised a debate over the bill in parliament on Sunday, saying that it is contrary to the Quran and Sunnah. They are saying that Islamic laws relating to inheritance, wills and hiba will all be affected.

Asaduzzaman: It is specifically mentioned in Section 122 (A)(4). Regardless of whether there is a hiba, gift or any other format under other laws, it will not be affected or restricted by this law.

Bangladesh is home to people of various religions, including Muslims, Hindus, Buddhists and Christians. Will the law apply to people of all religions?

Asaduzzaman: Yes, that is why it has been enacted. It will apply to Bangladeshis. It will apply to matters concerning property in Bangladesh.

Property and inheritance laws differ among religions. Will there not be any contradiction in applying the law to everyone?

Asaduzzaman: There will be no contradiction. If someone wants to follow their religion, the law will not stand in their way. Anyone who wishes to do so can. An option has been kept in the law. We have also specifically mentioned that in the sub-section 4.

Did you consult or speak with Islamic scholars at any stage before enacting the law?

Asaduzzaman: We spoke informally with a few people. I even spoke with the person from Jamaat whom I mentioned, Shishir Monir—he is a good lawyer. I spoke with him as well. He also said, “I do not see anything wrong here.”

You said in parliament that this law does not touch upon Muslim law. What will be the difference between hiba, which is customary among Muslims, and a gift under this law? Will hiba remain?

Asaduzzaman: Of course, hiba will remain. I have stated that in the law itself. Section 122(A)( 4), clearly states this. It will not only leave hiba untouched; it will also not affect the personal laws of other religions. Everything is protected.

The Opposition is opposing this law, and other religious organisations, including Hefazat-e-Islam, have also issued statements expressing their reactions. Are you feeling any religious pressure over the law?

Asaduzzaman: I do not see that as pressure. They have given their interpretations. I think it is their misinterpretation. On the one hand, they are saying that this law is against Islam. On the other hand, they are saying that an amendment should be brought to include a provision that the 1937 law will also apply here.

But the Opposition said on Sunday that the government is giving a misinterpretation.

Asaduzzaman: I do not think so. We have spoken with references. On this particular point of the law, we have given references to laws from around the world. We have cited references from Malaysia, Jordan, Saudi Arabia, the UAE (United Arab Emirates), the Privy Council, the Indian Supreme Court and the Pakistani courts. We have made this clear.

Suppose a father gives his house as a gift to his son. But under the new law, the father will use the house while he is alive. So who is the legal owner—the father or the son?

Asaduzzaman: The son. The moment the gift is made, the son becomes the owner.

What happens if the son does not allow the donor to exercise the right of usufruct?

Asaduzzaman: We have kept an option there. He can directly file a petition with the district judge.

So then, just as they have to go to court under the Maintenance Act, they would have to go to court here as well...

Asaduzzaman: That will be very rare because this law has been made so clear that no son will be able to take advantage of that opportunity.

Can the donor later sell, mortgage or otherwise transfer the property they have given away to someone else? If so, where would the recipient’s rights stand?

Asaduzzaman: No, they cannot. They can only enjoy the property. This is where the difference from hiba lies.

Is there a concern that someone could use this law to bypass inheritance laws and devise a new way of distributing property during their lifetime?

Asaduzzaman: I do not see that at present.

If a father gives all his property to one child while retaining the right to enjoy it during his lifetime, will the other children still have an opportunity to inherit?

Asaduzzaman: That is also possible under hiba. If a father decides to give all his property to one son, he can do that under hiba as well.

Would this contradict Islamic law, meaning the inheritance law as it exists in our country?

Asaduzzaman: It does not contradict it at all. As an example, we have said that the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance of 1961 introduced several changes. They were landmark changes. Suppose I have an only child. My child dies before me. If I had died first, that child would have inherited under Islamic law. But if the child dies first, their children, the minor children, would not receive my share. They would not receive what their father would have inherited from me. In 1961, the law states – no, the share that child would have received will go to their children.

Then, suppose under Islamic law, saying “three talaqs” orally results in a divorce. The 1961 law said – no, saying three talaqs does not mean that the divorce will take effect immediately.”

Third, suppose a husband and wife get divorced. If they wanted to marry each other again, there was a provision requiring a halala marriage. The 1961 law said –  no, there will be no such thing as a halala marriage. The divorce has become final. If they wish to do so later, they can marry each other again.

If the law applies equally to Muslims, has any special protection been included in the bill to avoid potential conflict with Muslim inheritance law?

Asaduzzaman: Yes, it has.

What is that?

Asaduzzaman: The provision in Section 122(A)( 4), says that none of those laws will in any way be obstructed by this law.

The opposition alleges that Shariah provisions are being bypassed in an attempt to solve a social problem.

Asaduzzaman: That is incorrect. An opposition MP sent me an opinion from a scholar today (Monday). The opinion says that conditions cannot be imposed on hiba. I am also saying that no conditions can be imposed on hiba. That is why I am leaving hiba untouched. This is Islamic law—I have not interfered with it.

Now, regarding this property that will be given under the new provision, there is the existing practice of giving property through hiba. What will be the procedure for giving it?

Asaduzzaman: It will have to be registered, in the same way as hiba is registered.

What will this registration be called?

Asaduzzaman: That will be a gift. In English, it is called a ‘gift’.

Some people are also concerned that the new provision could lead to an increase in property-related lawsuits in the courts.

Asaduzzaman: It will reduce them further.

Is there any explanation for how the number of property-related lawsuits will decrease?

Asaduzzaman: Because when it is clearly stated that the donor will retain the right to enjoy the property during their lifetime, the children, when they see it that way, will not dispute it. Since the ownership has already been decided, the number of lawsuits over this will not increase in any way. They will be discouraged from going to court.

Have references from other countries around the world been incorporated into this law?

Asaduzzaman: We have included references from other countries. We have said that provisions for such separate gifts, outside hiba, exist in various Muslim countries around the world. For example, we have cited Saudi Arabia, Malaysia and the UAE. The Privy Council even addressed this in 1922. It was not about a law of this kind; rather, it said that if a person retains a usufruct right at the time of making a hiba, that would not make the hiba invalid.

Would you like to say anything to those opposing this law or to Islamic scholars?

Asaduzzaman: I would tell the Opposition: Please read the law carefully, understand it properly, and recognise that the responsibility of children towards their parents is gradually declining. Come back from the position of giving an misinterpretation of this law, which has been introduced specifically to protect parents from this declining sense of responsibility.

My message to Islamic scholars is very clear. You are saying that hiba has been touched by this law—I am saying that hiba has not been touched. Please look carefully at Section 122(A)(4). It clearly states that this law will neither affect nor touch hiba, or the mode of transfer under Islamic or other religions, or any other method provided for under other laws.

Do you think any changes or additions to this law are necessary?

Asaduzzaman: At present, I do not see any. If any problems arise in the practical field in the future, we will look into them then.

If any proposal comes from the Opposition as well, will there be an opportunity to include it in this case?

Asaduzzaman: If something positive comes up and we feel that there is scope to consider it from a legal perspective, it will certainly be taken into consideration.

Thank you for giving us your time.

Md Asaduzzaman: Thanks to Prothom Alo as well.

item.title: “I’m not easy to silence”: Actress Badhon attacked and harassed in Italy
item.description:
Actress Azmeri Haque Badhon says she was attacked and harassed in Italy, where she was allegedly pelted with water, soft drinks and eggs and physically assaulted.

Badhon also said her mobile phone was knocked out of her hand. Her brother’s young child was with them during the incident. She later filed a complaint with the local police.

Badhon alleged that she was targeted because of her active role in the student-people’s movement of July–August 2024. She said some of the attackers identified themselves as activists of the Awami League, whose activities are currently banned, and the banned Bangladesh Chhatra League, as well as “soldiers of Bangabandhu”.

According to the actress, the attackers forced her to say, “Joy Bangla, Joy Bangabandhu”. They also attempted to record the incident and livestream and publish the footage on social media, she alleged.

Badhon travelled to Italy to attend a screening of The Difficult Bride, directed by Rubaiyat Hossain, at the 83rd Venice International Film Festival. She is currently staying in Mestre. The attack and harassment took place on Monday night when she went to a local park with her brother and his family.

After the incident, Badhon went live on her verified Facebook page and described what had happened in detail. She later posted several videos of the attack and harassment.

The videos show several people approaching Badhon aggressively, grappling with her and speaking to her angrily. Some of them can be heard calling her a “July Jongi” (July terror).

Speaking during Facebook Live, Badhon said, “I went to the park with my brother’s family. A lot of our Bangladeshi brothers came there and physically harassed me. They threw water and Coke at me. I was completely drenched.”

Badhon said she was hit and struck near her ear. “They hit me, knocked my phone out of my hand and struck me near my ear.”

Her brother’s young child was also present during the incident. In one of the videos she posted, the child can be heard trying to stop the attackers. In response, one person can be heard saying, “What child? He has to say Joy Bangla.”

Several people can also be heard in the videos calling Badhon a “July terror” and making aggressive remarks about her political position.

“They called me a July warrior. Yes, I am. I certainly took part in the July movement,” Badhon said.

Badhon also said her sister-in-law was pushed during the incident. “I was hit, and my brother’s wife was also pushed,” she said.

Condemning the incident, Badhon said, “It will not be so easy to silence Azmeri Haque Badhon. Today, you showed people around the world that an actress representing Bangladesh was harassed.”

Addressing the attackers, she added, “You should have moved on from this irrational behaviour, but you could not. You thought that perhaps by behaving this way, you could rebuild your position later. I do not think that is going to happen.”

In her video message, Badhon also mentioned Sajeeb Wazed Joy, the son of ousted prime minister Sheikh Hasina. She said she had learned that Joy was also in Venice and asked for the incident to be brought to his attention.

Badhon was active on the streets during the student-people’s movement of July–August 2024 and spoke to local and international media in support of the movement.

Badhon is attending the Venice International Film Festival with the team of The Difficult Bride. Directed by Rubaiyat Hossain, the film has been selected for the festival’s Orizzonti section. Its world premiere was held at the Sala Darsena theatre on 6 September. The film stars Zainen Karim, Rikita Nandini Shimu, Sunerah Binte Kamal and Azmeri Haque Badhon in its four principal female roles.

item.title: Dinesh Trivedi: PM Tarique has a standing invitation
item.description:
Indian High Commissioner to Bangladesh Dinesh Trivedi on Monday expressed optimism that Prime Minister Tarique Rahman would pay a visit to India at the right time, stressing that the Prime Minister knows about the standing invitation.
"We are absolutely confident....at the right time... the prime minister of Bangladesh has a standing invitation, and he knows it," he told reporters when a journalist wanted to know about the possible visit.
The high commissioner met with Environment, Forest and Climate Change Minister Abdul Awal Mintoo.
State Minister Shaikh Faridul Islam was also present.
Talking to reporters after the meeting, the high commissioner said the people-to-people relationship is very important.
"So, we don't only share borders, we share dreams," he said.
The Indian envoy said environment and animals, fortunately, do not require visas.
They discussed the progress of bilateral cooperation mechanisms in the areas of wildlife conservation and habitat protection, as well as opportunities to further strengthen cooperation on transboundary pollution, waste management, and other environmental issues of mutual interest.
Regarding Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s possible visit to India, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir on Saturday said the possibility of such a visit before the UN General Assembly session is slim.
"When the time is right, the prime minister will be visiting India, but the possibility is very slim before the UNGA as the Prime Minister will be attending the UNGA," he told reporters in Sylhet.

item.title: Study: Second-hand smoke causes to nearly 1.7m deaths globally
item.description:
More than 2.7 billion people, including children, have been exposed to second-hand smoke globally, contributing to nearly 1.7 million deaths in 2023, according to a study published Tuesday in The Lancet.
Tobacco remains a leading cause of disease globally, the study said, noting many "non-smokers exposed to second-hand smoke" were among the estimate total of 8 million people who died in 2023 of smoking-related illnesses.
"Exposure to second-hand smoke is a globally recognised health risk, with no safe level of inhalation," it said.
By reviewing studies published in the US National Institutes of Health database PubMed along with population surveys, Tuesday's study sought to estimate the prevalence of exposure to second-hand smoke and quantify the burden of disease in 204 countries and territories between 1990 and 2023.
Among the approximately 2.7 billion people exposed to second-hand smoke in 2023 were 767 million children aged 0 to 14, the study found.
This exposure is estimated to have resulted in 1.66 million premature deaths and caused premature disability and illness, leading to ischemic heart disease, a heart condition caused by insufficient oxygen supply to the heart muscle.
In children, exposure to second-hand smoke is estimated to have caused 5.2 million respiratory tract infections in 2023, it said.
People in proximity to someone lighting up are exposed to both the "sidestream smoke" from the burning tobacco product and smoke exhaled by the active smoker, the study explained.
"The sidestream component, which dominates the air non-smokers breathe, is unfiltered... carrying higher per-unit concentrations of the toxic and carcinogenic compounds" than that being inhaled by the active smoker, it said.
Despite significant declines in smoking prevalence globally since 1990, the absolute number of people exposed has remained stable due to population growth and increased exposure in Africa and the Middle East.
Women are also disproportionately affected by second-hand smoke, particularly in regions where smoking prevalence among women is low, it noted.
"Despite this substantial burden, (second-hand smoke) exposure remains rarely acknowledged as a major risk factor for female health," it said.
The study called for governments to implement stronger tobacco controls in public places and in homes in order to better protect women and children from second-hand smoke.

item.title: Bangladesh’s literacy future begins before first grade
item.description:
On the 60th anniversary of International Literacy Day, Bangladesh stands at an important point in its education journey. According to the Bangladesh Sample Vital Statistics 2023: Key Findings report, the national literacy rate among people aged seven and above rose to 77.9%, from 58.6% in 2014.
Yet these gains do not tell the whole story. Functional literacy, the ability to read, write, think critically, and apply knowledge in daily life, remains out of reach for millions.
According to the World Bank’s Human Capital Index 2020, 58% of 10-year-olds in Bangladesh are unable to read and understand a simple text by the end of primary school.
That is more than one in every two children.
One important part of this challenge begins even before children enter primary school.
A study by Nirmala, Umayahara, Yang and Ranganathan (2021) shows that up to 80-85% of children from the poorest socioeconomic quintiles enter Class 1 without adequate pre-literacy exposure, structured storytelling, or formal early childhood education.
When children enter primary school without these foundations, they are expected to cope immediately with a fast-paced curriculum. This can lead to early frustration and poor comprehension.
Children from disadvantaged backgrounds are three times more likely to drop out of primary school than their wealthiest peers. This, in turn, can reinforce an intergenerational cycle of poverty and weaken the country’s human resources.
The gap is even wider for children with disabilities. They often face multiple barriers, including negative attitudes, delayed enrolment, and a lack of adapted learning materials. These obstacles can exclude them from the literacy journey before it has properly begun.
Children do not all learn and develop at the same pace or in the same way. Using fixed developmental milestones to decide whether a child is “ready” for school can unfairly disadvantage children with disabilities. Yet with appropriate support, every child can learn and participate.
Early lessons from the GPE KIX- and IDRC Canada-supported EN-REACH Education implementation research project, being conducted in selected government primary schools in Kushtia and Gaibandha districts, suggest that school readiness cannot be strengthened by focusing on the child alone.
The support surrounding the child, particularly from teachers, parents, and other caregivers, also matters.
Preliminary qualitative findings suggest that children with disabilities who were initially shy or anxious became more confident and engaged when they experienced language-rich, play-based learning at home and in school.
Teachers also reported that inclusive, play-based approaches designed to support children with disabilities benefited other children in the classroom as well.
The research is also showing the value of equipping pre-primary teachers with practical skills for inclusive teaching and of using low-cost, locally-available play materials.
At home, involving fathers, grandparents, and community members in school-readiness activities can broaden responsibility for early learning and help build a more supportive and gender-equitable environment for children.
These emerging lessons point to a wider conclusion: Inclusive pre-primary education works best when the classroom, home, and community reinforce one another, rather than when school readiness is treated solely as the responsibility of the child or teacher.
But promising approaches in a few settings will not be enough unless quality pre-primary education becomes more widely accessible. Across Bangladesh, access to quality early education remains deeply unequal.
First , Bangladesh needs to invest more in early education. Expanding preschool enrollment in low- and middle-income countries could generate benefit-to-cost ratios ranging from 6.4 to 17.6.
Yet Bangladesh spends just over 2% of GDP on education, well below Unesco’s recommended 4% to 6%. A significant, protected share of increased education spending should go to pre-primary education in marginalized communities.
Second , inclusion and play-based learning need to become central to pre-primary education.
Classrooms should have age-appropriate reading materials in children’s mother tongues, interactive toys, and storybooks. Pre-primary education should also move away from excessive memorization and give children more opportunities to learn through play, stories, interaction, and exploration.
Third , the pre-primary workforce needs to be professionalized. Teaching young children, particularly children with disabilities, requires specialized pedagogical skills. This should receive proper attention in education planning, budgeting and implementation.
Finally , evidence-based inclusive models need to be scaled up. As stronger evidence emerges on effective ways to include children with disabilities and engage fathers in early learning, the Ministry of Primary and Mass Education, the National Curriculum and Textbook Board, and development partners should consider how these practices can be incorporated into national policy.
If Bangladesh wants a population capable of succeeding in a digital economy, participating meaningfully in society and escaping poverty, investment must begin when the human brain is developing most rapidly.
By ensuring universal, high-quality, play-based and inclusive pre-primary education for every child, Bangladesh can make sure that improvements in literacy are not simply reflected in statistics, but in the knowledge, skills and opportunities of its people.
Utpal Mallick is an Assistant Program Manager at icddr,b and can be reached at utpal.mallick@icddrb.org .

item.title: From a refugee camp in Cox’s Bazar to New York University
item.description:
When I fled Myanmar in 2017, I carried very little with me. My family escaped violence, persecution, and fear.
We walked for days through forests and mountains before reaching Bangladesh. Along the way, we lost our home, our security, and the future we had imagined.
But there was one thing I refused to leave behind: My belief in education.
Today, on World Literacy Day, we often think about literacy as the ability to read and write. For refugees, it means much more.
Literacy can mean understanding your rights, accessing reliable information, communicating with the world beyond a refugee camp, challenging misinformation, and finding the confidence to speak for yourself.
For me, education became one of the most powerful forms of protection.
As a Rohingya refugee in Bangladesh, I watched thousands of young people grow up with extremely limited access to formal education. They had dreams of becoming doctors, teachers, engineers, lawyers, and community leaders.
Displacement did not take away their talent or ambition. It took away their opportunities.
This distinction matters.
Refugees do not choose to become refugees. No child chooses to flee war, persecution, or violence. Yet once displaced, refugee children are often expected to carry the consequences of decisions they never made.
They encounter restrictions on movement, lack of legal documentation, poverty, discrimination, language barriers, and limited pathways to higher education.
The result is not simply an education crisis. It is a loss of human potential.
When a young person spends years in a refugee camp without meaningful access to education, we should not ask why that person has failed to progress. We should ask why the systems around them failed to provide an opportunity.
I know what that feels like.
For years, I tried to find a way to continue my education while living as a stateless Rohingya refugee in Bangladesh. There were moments when the possibility of attending a university seemed almost impossible.
I had the desire to learn. I was willing to work. What I did not have was the legal status and opportunity that most students take for granted.
Yet I continued.
In 2024, after seven years as a refugee in Bangladesh, I came to the United States as a student. This year, I graduated from New York University with a bachelor's degree in social science, concentrating in international studies.
My journey from a refugee camp in Cox's Bazar to a university classroom in New York has taught me something important: Talent is universal, but opportunity is not.
I am not the only Rohingya young person capable of reaching a university. There are students in the refugee camps today who could become doctors, lawyers, teachers, entrepreneurs, researchers, diplomats, and leaders.
But talent cannot substitute indefinitely for access.
Through the Rohingya Student Network, which I founded while living in the refugee camp, I have seen what happens when young people are given opportunities to learn.
Education does more than transfer knowledge. It builds confidence. It develops leadership. It gives people the tools to understand the forces shaping their lives and the ability to participate in decisions about their future.
That is why literacy should also be understood as a question of power.
A person who can access information, evaluate it critically, understand their rights, communicate their ideas, and tell their own story is harder to silence.
For a stateless community whose identity and history have repeatedly been denied or misrepresented, that matters enormously.
Literacy also matters in the digital age. Refugees increasingly receive news, communicate, organize, study, and understand events through phones and social media.
Being literate today therefore requires more than reading words on a page. Young people must also be able to distinguish information from misinformation, understand how digital platforms influence what they see, and use technology responsibly.
For the Rohingya, these skills are particularly important. We have already witnessed the devastating consequences of misinformation, hate speech, and dehumanizing narratives.
Education must therefore prepare young people not only for employment but also to think critically, challenge hatred, engage peacefully with others, and become responsible participants in their communities.
The international community often speaks about durable solutions for refugees. Education must be at the centre of that conversation.
Investing in refugee education is not charity. It is one of the smartest investments governments, universities, and donors can make in human potential.
Educated refugees contribute to economies, strengthen communities, promote social cohesion, and help build peace.
They become problem-solvers rather than being viewed solely through the lens of humanitarian need.
My life changed because people and institutions eventually saw beyond my refugee status and recognized my potential as a student. That should not be an exceptional story.
On this World Literacy Day, I hope we move beyond asking how many refugee children can read and write. We should ask a much bigger question: How many have been given the education necessary to determine their own future?
Food keeps people alive. Shelter provides safety. Humanitarian assistance helps people survive displacement.
But education gives people the tools to move beyond survival.
For a refugee, a book can be more than a book. A classroom can be more than a classroom. And literacy can be more than the ability to read and write.
It can be the beginning of freedom.
Maung Sawyedollah is a Rohingya student and activist currently living in New York City. He graduated from New York University this spring with a BA in social science and is currently preparing to start a JD.

item.title: Farmer killed, two injured in Kushtia lightning strike
item.description:
A farmer was killed, and two others were seriously injured in a lightning strike in the Tegharia area under Kanchanpur union of Sadar upazila on Monday afternoon.
The deceased was Toafazzel Hossain, 55, son of Mannan Pradhan of Swastipur village under Alampur union of Sadar upazila.
According to police and local sources, Toafazzel was returning home from his crop field. When he reached the Tegharia field, lightning suddenly struck him around 2pm, leaving him dead on the spot.
Two other people were also seriously injured in the lightning strike. Locals rescued them and admitted them to Kushtia Medical College Hospital.
Alampur Police Camp in-charge ASI Faridul Islam confirmed the matter.

item.title: KCC announces Tk 601.79cr budget for FY 2026-27
item.description:
The Khulna City Corporation (KCC) has proposed a budget of Tk 601.79 crore for the 2026-27 fiscal year, without imposing any new taxes.
KCC Administrator Nazrul Islam Manju on Monday announced the budget at the Shaheed Altaf Auditorium of the Nagar Bhaban.
The proposed budget has a deficit of Tk 29.54 crore as expenditure exceeds projected revenue.
Of the total budget, Tk 211.90 crore has been projected as revenue income against Tk 241.44 crore in revenue expenditure. Government grants under the second component have been estimated at Tk 197.62 crore.
For the 2025-26 fiscal year, KCC had initially set a budget target of Tk 719.50 crore, which was revised to Tk 338.97 crore.
The achievement rate was 71.70 percent for the own-fund component and 38.52 percent for the development fund, with an overall achievement rate of 47.12 percent.
Although the budget has been described as development-oriented, it is largely dependent on government and donor grants as well as the corporation’s own revenue.
Manju attributed the shortfall mainly to changes in the country’s political situation and completion of several major projects.
He said Tk 79.46 crore has been allocated under the special development fund for the current fiscal year, while Tk 150 crore has been earmarked under the Annual Development Programme (ADP).
Of the ADP allocation, Tk 92.87 crore has been earmarked for physical infrastructure, Tk 20.50 crore for public health, Tk 33.13 crore for conservancy, Tk 2 crore for emergency water supply and Tk 1.50 crore for veterinary services.
KCC also plans to plant around 50,000 trees and undertake climate-resilient infrastructure development in low-income settlements, including roads, drains, culverts and latrines.
Manju said Tk 73.36 crore had been allocated from KCC’s own funds for development after meeting its regular establishment costs. Of this, Tk 55.27 crore has been earmarked for infrastructure, BMDF, street lighting, education, sports and culture, social welfare, environment, public health, veterinary and conservancy sectors.
